assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Habitat
items.clue: The place in which a community, species, population or organism lives.

items.label: Abiotic variable
items.clue: A non-living factor of the environment that can vary from place to place or over time and affect where a species can live.

items.label: Pneumatophore
items.clue: A vertical root that grows upward from the horizontal roots of a mangrove such as Avicennia marina and projects above the mud into the air.

items.label: Zooxanthellae
items.clue: Photosynthetic unicellular algae (dinoflagellates) that live inside the tissues of reef-building coral polyps in a mutualistic relationship.

questions.stem: Which statement gives the meaning of the term habitat as it is used in ecology?

options.text: The place in which a community, species, population or single organism lives.
The role that a species plays in its ecosystem, including what it feeds on.
A large region of the Earth that shares one type of climate, such as tundra.
The set of organisms of different species that live together in one area.

questions.explanation: This is the definition used in the guide. A habitat is a place, and it can be the place where a whole community lives or where one organism lives; it is described by geographical location, physical location and ecosystem type.

questions.stem: Which statement about abiotic variables and the distribution of species is correct?

options.text: Only the distribution of plants is limited by abiotic variables, because animals are able to move away from unfavourable conditions.
A species with a wide range of tolerance for temperature is found everywhere that the temperature lies within that range.
Adaptations give a species a range of tolerance for each abiotic variable, and it is absent where a variable is outside that range.
An abiotic variable is any feature of the environment, whether it is living or non-living, that differs between one place and another.

questions.stem: Students are required to collect transect data from a natural or semi-natural habitat. Which of these sites is semi-natural?

options.text: A hay meadow that is cut once each year but is dominated by wild grasses and wildflowers.
A field of wheat grown from sown seed, with wild poppies growing along its margins.
A garden lawn sown with a bought seed mixture and mown every week through the summer.
A peat bog in a remote upland with no history of drainage, grazing or other management.

questions.stem: Which statement about the conditions needed for a coral reef to form is correct?

options.text: The water must be deep, so that the coral polyps are shielded from the damaging effects of bright sunlight.
The water should be turbid and rich in suspended sediment, which supplies food to the polyps.
The water must be shallow and clear enough for light to reach the zooxanthellae in the coral tissue.
The water should be as warm as possible, because calcification speeds up with every rise in temperature.

questions.stem: A biome has long, very cold winters, a growing season of only a few weeks, precipitation below about 250 mm a year and permanently frozen subsoil. Which biome is this?

options.text: Taiga, as in northern Canada
Hot desert, as in Arabia
Tundra, as in Arctic Canada
Grassland, as on the prairies

questions.explanation: Very cold temperatures, a growing season of a few weeks, very low precipitation and permafrost are the climate conditions that characterize tundra, which supports low-growing plants but no trees.

questions.stem: What is the role of ATP in the cross-bridge cycle of muscle contraction?

options.text: ATP is hydrolysed to power the pull of the head on actin; when ATP is used up the heads let go and the muscle relaxes.
One ATP is hydrolysed at the start of a contraction; the heads then ratchet along the actin without ever detaching.
Binding of ATP releases the myosin head from actin, and its hydrolysis re-cocks the head for the next cycle.
ATP is not used by the myosin head; the power stroke is driven by calcium ions binding directly to it.

questions.stem: What are the roles of the protein titin in a sarcomere?

options.text: It acts as an elastic spring that returns a stretched sarcomere to its resting length and stiffens to stop it being overstretched.
It forms a third set of filaments that shorten actively to help pull the Z lines together during contraction.
It pulls a contracted sarcomere back out to its resting length, so that an antagonistic muscle is not required.
It is a rigid, inextensible cable from Z line to M line that stops the sarcomere from stretching at all.

questions.stem: What is a motor unit in skeletal muscle?

options.text: One motor neuron and the single muscle fibre it contacts at one neuromuscular junction.
A whole muscle together with the single motor neuron that stimulates it to contract.
One motor neuron and all of the muscle fibres that its branching axon stimulates.
A muscle fibre fused to its motor neuron so that impulses pass straight into it.

questions.explanation: The axon of a motor neuron branches to form a neuromuscular junction with each of many muscle fibres. The neuron and every fibre it supplies form one motor unit, and all of those fibres contract together when the neuron fires.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the roles of structures in the human hip joint?

options.text: Tendons join the pelvis to the femur and hold the joint together, and ligaments attach the muscles that move it to the bones.
Ligaments join the pelvis to the femur and stabilize the joint, and tendons attach the muscles that move it to the bones.
Cartilage covering the head of the femur secretes the synovial fluid that lubricates the joint and reduces friction.
The head of the femur rocks against the pelvis in a single plane, so the hip is a hinge joint like the knee.

questions.stem: Which example of locomotion is correctly matched with its reason?

options.text: A young spider being carried away from its hatching site on a long thread of silk: migration.
A male emperor moth flying upwind along the trail of pheromone released by a female: searching for a mate.
A humpback whale swimming from polar feeding grounds to tropical waters where it does not feed: foraging for food.
A wildebeest herd crossing the Serengeti as seasonal rains and fresh grazing move: escaping from danger.

questions.stem: How does the way a dolphin propels itself differ from the way a bony fish such as a tuna does?

options.text: Both tails beat from side to side; the dolphin's fluke is horizontal so that it can also act as a hydroplane.
The dolphin rows itself along with its flippers, while the tuna's thrust comes from its tail fin.
The dolphin's horizontal fluke beats up and down; the tuna's vertical tail fin beats from side to side.
The dolphin's flippers and fluke are fins of the same kind as the tuna's, so the two swim in the same way.
